cards.meaning: Giving the important information clearly, in as few words as possible.
cards.nuance: Pure praise for writing and speaking. Asking someone to be more concise is a gentle way to say they ramble.

uses.sentence: Keep the summary concise: three bullets, one ask, and the deadline.
uses.tip: Pair it with a concrete limit so people know what concise means to you.

uses.sentence: To put it concisely: we’re late, it’s raining, and I’ve found a bar.
uses.tip: “To put it concisely” works as a funny setup for a quick summary.

uses.where: Feedback on a report · comment in the margin
uses.sentence: Great analysis, but the intro could be more concise; cut the history and lead with the finding.
uses.tip: Soften it by praising the content first.

origin.summary: From Latin concisus, ‘cut up, cut short’, from concidere, built on caedere, ‘to cut’.

timeline.text: concidere, ‘to cut up’.
Enters English for brief, compact speech or writing.
A core quality of good business writing.

cards.pitfall: Concise means short and clear; precise means exact. A message can be one without the other.

cards.meaning: Possible to do in practice, given the time, money and people available.
cards.nuance: More grounded than possible: it asks whether we can realistically pull it off. Not feasible is a polite no.

uses.sentence: Launching by Friday isn’t feasible without dropping the reporting feature.
uses.tip: Say what would make it feasible, not just that it isn’t.

uses.sentence: Is it even feasible to drive there and back in a day with the kids?
uses.tip: Works for any plan that might be too ambitious.

uses.sentence: We recommend a two-week study to test the feasibility of moving suppliers.
uses.tip: A feasibility study checks whether a plan can work before you commit.

origin.summary: From Old French faisible, ‘that can be done’, from faire, ‘to do’, which comes from Latin facere.

timeline.text: facere, ‘to do, make’.
faisible, ‘doable’.
Enters English with the same meaning.

cards.pitfall: Feasible means can be done, not likely to happen; a plan can be feasible and still a bad idea.

cards.meaning: To make something bad less severe, harmful or painful.
cards.nuance: Sounds calm and in control. It admits a problem exists while showing you have a plan to reduce it.

uses.sentence: To mitigate the risk of delays, we’ll order the hardware this week.
uses.tip: Name the risk, then the action that mitigates it.

uses.where: Chatting with a neighbor · noisy renovation
uses.sentence: We’re doing the loud work before noon to mitigate the noise for everyone.
uses.tip: A slightly formal but friendly way to show consideration.

uses.sentence: The impact was mitigated by switching traffic to the backup region within ten minutes.
uses.tip: Common in reports; follow it with the specific step taken.

origin.summary: From Latin mitigare, ‘to soften, make mild’, from mitis, ‘mild, gentle’.

timeline.text: mitis, ‘mild’; mitigare, ‘to make mild’.
Enters English for easing pain or punishment.
Standard in risk, safety and business language.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse it with militate (against), which means to be a strong factor preventing something.

cards.meaning: To give part of your work, responsibility or authority to someone else.
cards.nuance: A sign of trust and good management when done well; it can feel like dumping work if you only pass on the boring parts.

uses.sentence: You can’t do every review yourself; delegate the smaller ones to Leo and Ana.
uses.tip: Delegate the outcome, not just the task, so people own it.

uses.sentence: I’ve delegated drinks to my brother, so I only have to worry about the food.
uses.tip: Playful at home; it makes chores sound like management.

uses.sentence: While I’m away, approvals are delegated to Chris, who can sign off anything under budget.
uses.tip: Make clear who has authority, not just who is around.

origin.summary: From Latin delegare, ‘to send away, entrust’, from de-, ‘away’, and legare, ‘to send as an envoy’.

timeline.text: legare, ‘to appoint, send as envoy’.
Delegate enters English as a noun for a representative.
The verb, ‘to entrust to another’, follows.

cards.pitfall: The verb ends in ‘gate’ (DEL-uh-gate); the noun, a representative, ends in ‘git’ (DEL-uh-git).

cards.meaning: Forming a united whole; working well together as one group or piece.
cards.nuance: Positive and team-focused. Often used about teams, designs and stories that hang together.

uses.sentence: The new squad is finally feeling cohesive, and handoffs have gotten much faster.
uses.tip: Good for describing team health without sounding fluffy.

uses.sentence: If we keep the wood tones, the living room will look more cohesive.
uses.tip: Common in design talk for things that match and belong together.

uses.sentence: Using one font family keeps our materials cohesive across web and print.
uses.tip: Explains why consistency rules matter.

origin.summary: From Latin cohaerere, ‘to stick together’, from co-, ‘together’, and haerere, ‘to stick’. Cohere and adhere share the root.

timeline.text: haerere, ‘to stick’; cohaerere, ‘to stick together’.
Cohesion appears in English, first in physics.
Cohesive is used for things and groups that hold together.

cards.pitfall: Cohesive means sticking together as a group; coherent means logical and easy to follow.

cards.meaning: Real and clear enough to be seen, measured or proven, not just talked about.
cards.nuance: Pushes vague talk toward real results. Literally it means something you can touch.

uses.sentence: Let’s agree on one tangible outcome for this quarter, like cutting support tickets by a fifth.
uses.tip: Ask for something tangible when a plan feels like buzzwords.

uses.where: Catching up · a friend’s new habit
uses.sentence: After a month of walking to work, she says the difference in her mood is tangible.
uses.tip: Use it for changes that are clearly noticeable.

uses.sentence: The project delivered tangible benefits, including forty new library cards in its first month.
uses.tip: Always follow tangible with an actual number or example.

origin.summary: From Late Latin tangibilis, ‘that can be touched’, from tangere, ‘to touch’. Tangent and contact share the root.

timeline.text: tangere, ‘to touch’.
Enters English meaning able to be touched.
Extends to ‘real, definite, measurable’.

cards.meaning: To decide which things are most important and deal with them first.
cards.nuance: Implies choosing, which means something else waits. Saying everything is a priority usually means nothing is.

uses.sentence: We can’t do all twelve, so let’s prioritize the three that block customers.
uses.tip: Say what you’re dropping as well as what you’re keeping.

uses.sentence: I’m prioritizing sleep this week, so I’ll skip Thursday drinks.
uses.tip: A kind, firm way to turn down plans.

uses.sentence: Could you help me prioritize? The audit and the launch are both due Friday.
uses.tip: Asking a manager to prioritize hands them the trade-off they own.

origin.summary: Built in English from priority, which comes via Medieval Latin prioritas from prior, ‘earlier, first’. The verb is a 20th-century coinage.

timeline.text: prior, ‘former, first’.
Priority enters English.
Prioritize appears, first criticized as jargon, now standard.

cards.pitfall: British English often spells it prioritise; pick one spelling and stick to it in a document.

cards.meaning: Able to work successfully and keep going, especially in practical or financial terms.
cards.nuance: Focuses on whether something can survive and last, not just start. Common for plans, businesses and options.

uses.sentence: At that price the subscription isn’t viable; we’d lose money on every customer.
uses.tip: Use it when the question is whether something can sustain itself.

uses.sentence: The night bus is the only viable option after midnight.
uses.tip: “The only viable option” is a very natural pairing.

uses.sentence: Early sign-ups suggest a viable market for weekend repair classes.
uses.tip: Support it with evidence such as numbers or early demand.

origin.summary: From French viable, ‘able to live’, from vie, ‘life’, which comes from Latin vita. It first described newborns and seeds able to survive.

timeline.text: vita, ‘life’.
Enters English for living things able to survive.
Extends to plans and ideas that can work.

cards.pitfall: Feasible asks whether it can be done; viable asks whether it can keep working once it is.

cards.meaning: To express an idea or feeling clearly in words.
cards.nuance: Suggests turning something fuzzy into something clear. Useful when you or others are struggling to explain.

uses.sentence: Something feels off but I can’t articulate it yet; give me a minute to look again.
uses.tip: An honest way to buy time without dismissing your instinct.

uses.sentence: You articulated exactly what I’ve been feeling about my job.
uses.tip: A warm compliment when someone puts your thoughts into words.

uses.sentence: This document aims to articulate why we are moving to a single product line.
uses.tip: Common in mission and strategy writing.

origin.summary: From Latin articulatus, ‘jointed, divided into distinct parts’, from articulus, ‘small joint’. Clear speech is speech divided into distinct sounds.

timeline.text: articulus, ‘small joint’, from artus, ‘joint’.
Enters English for jointed things and distinct speech.
Mostly means expressing ideas clearly.

cards.pitfall: The adjective (good at speaking) ends in ‘-lit’; the verb ends in ‘-late’. Praising someone as articulate can sound patronizing if it implies surprise.

cards.meaning: General agreement among a group of people.
cards.nuance: Suggests everyone can live with the decision, not that everyone loves it. Waiting for full consensus can slow teams down.

uses.sentence: I think we have consensus on vendor B, so let’s confirm in writing today.
uses.tip: Check out loud before assuming you have it.

uses.where: Friends choosing a restaurant · group chat
uses.sentence: The consensus seems to be Thai, unless anyone strongly objects.
uses.tip: “The consensus seems to be” moves a group to a choice gently.

uses.sentence: There was broad consensus on the timeline, but budget remains open.
uses.tip: Broad consensus signals most, not all, people agree.

origin.summary: From Latin consensus, ‘agreement’, from consentire, ‘to feel together, agree’, from con-, ‘together’, and sentire, ‘to feel’.

timeline.text: consentire, ‘to agree’.
Becomes common in English for group agreement.
Everyday in meetings and politics.

cards.pitfall: It’s spelled consensus, not concensus. And general consensus of opinion is redundant; consensus is enough.

cards.meaning: To examine something very carefully and in detail, often looking for problems.
cards.nuance: Implies close, critical attention. Being scrutinized can feel uncomfortable, so it sounds tougher than check.

uses.sentence: Legal will scrutinize every clause, so flag anything unusual before we send it.
uses.tip: A useful warning that something will face close review.

uses.where: Meeting the parents · telling a friend
uses.sentence: Her dad scrutinized me all evening, but I think I passed.
uses.tip: Fun for describing being sized up.

uses.sentence: The new contract will face public scrutiny when the council meets next week.
uses.tip: Face scrutiny and come under scrutiny are common phrases.

origin.summary: From Latin scrutinium, ‘a search’, from scrutari, ‘to search, examine’. That verb is often linked to scruta, ‘rags, trash’, as if picking through rubbish, though the link is uncertain.

timeline.text: scrutari, ‘to search carefully’.
Scrutiny enters English, first for vote counting and inquiry.
The verb scrutinize appears.

cards.pitfall: It means looking closely, not glancing; don’t say you scrutinized something you only skimmed.

cards.meaning: Acting early to prepare for or prevent a problem, instead of waiting to react.
cards.nuance: Real praise when tied to a specific action; on its own it can sound like empty office jargon.

uses.sentence: You were proactive about the security update, and it saved us a stressful weekend.
uses.tip: Name the action so the praise feels real.

uses.where: Chatting with a friend · health check
uses.sentence: I’m trying to be more proactive about my health, so I booked a check-up.
uses.tip: Works well for personal habits and admin.

uses.sentence: We’re proactively letting you know that the app will be down on Sunday morning.
uses.tip: Shows customers you’re ahead of the problem.

origin.summary: Formed from pro-, ‘before’, and active. It began as a psychology term and became popular in business in the late 1900s.

timeline.text: Used in psychology, as in proactive inhibition.
Spreads into management and self-help writing.
Standard workplace vocabulary.

cards.pitfall: Overused in job ads and reviews; show proactive behavior with an example rather than just claiming it.
